yangon: Yangon stands in Lower Burma where the Yangon and Bago Rivers meet, about 30 km from the Gulf of Martaban, on the delta of the Irrawaddy. The name comes from the Burmese words yan, meaning enemies, and koun, meaning run out of, and is usually translated as End of Strife. The English form Rangoon is based on the Rakhine dialect. In 1989 the military government changed the city's English name to Yangon, along with many other transliterations; many Burmese did not accept the changes, and neither did a number of publications and foreign governments.

The settlement was founded as Dagon by the Mon people, who then inhabited Lower Burma, in the early 11th century (c. 1028-1043). From the 14th century, under the Hanthawaddy kingdom, it became an important pilgrimage town around its pagoda. Princess Maha Dewi governed it from 1364 to 1392, and her grandniece Shin Saw Pu, later the only female queen regnant in Burmese history, built a palace beside the Shwedagon Pagoda in 1460 and lived there until her death in 1471.

The British captured Yangon and all of Lower Burma in the Second Anglo-Burmese War of 1852 and made the city the commercial and political centre of British Burma, moving the capital there from Moulmein. On a design by the army engineer Lt. Alexander Fraser, they laid out a new city on a grid plan on delta land, bounded on the east by the Pazundaung Creek and on the south and west by the Yangon River. After the Third Anglo-Burmese War of 1885 it became the capital of all British-ruled Burma. By the 1890s prosperous suburbs had grown north of Royal Lake (Kandawgyi) and Inya Lake, and the British had founded hospitals and colleges, among them Rangoon General Hospital and Rangoon University.

After independence in 1948 many colonial names of streets and parks were replaced by Burmese ones. The city's area grew from 72.52 square kilometres in 1901 to 208.51 in 1974 and 598.75 in 2008, as it spread north towards the airport.

Yangon is the capital of the Yangon Region and the largest city of Myanmar, with about 5.16 million people at the 2014 census, and its main commercial centre. It was the national capital until the government moved its administration to the purpose-built Naypyidaw in 2005-2006. Its colonial-era core, centred on the Sule Pagoda, holds the largest number of colonial-period buildings in Southeast Asia, among them the former High Court, the former Secretariat and the Strand Hotel. The gilded Shwedagon Pagoda is the most sacred Buddhist pagoda of Myanmar. The main religions practised in the city are Buddhism, Christianity, Islam and Hinduism.
yangtze-river: The Yangtze, called Chang Jiang, or Long River, in Chinese, rises in the Tanggula Mountains of the Tibetan Plateau and flows for 6,300 kilometres in a generally easterly direction to the East China Sea. Its drainage basin comprises one-fifth of the land area of China. The source the Chinese government has traditionally recognised is the Tuotuo tributary at the base of a glacier on Geladandong Mountain, while the hydrologically longest source, at Jari Hill, was discovered only in the late 20th century. The river has over 700 tributaries, among them the Min, Jialing, Han and Gan, and it passes Chongqing, Wuhan and Nanjing on its way to Shanghai.

Unlike the Yellow River, whose mouth has shifted north and south of the Shandong peninsula, the Yangtze has remained largely static. Human activity is verified in the Three Gorges area as far back as 27,000 years ago. By the 5th millennium BCE the lower Yangtze was a major population centre of the Hemudu and Majiabang cultures, among the earliest cultivators of rice, followed in the 3rd millennium BCE by the Liangzhu culture. What is thought of as Chinese culture developed along the Yellow River, and the Yue of the lower Yangtze, who tattooed their bodies and cut their hair short, were considered barbarous by northerners.

Steamers came late to the upper river between Yichang and Chongqing, where the Three Gorges posed hazards of crosscurrents and whirlpools, and junks were pulled upriver by 70 to 80 trackers. The river was a major barrier between northern and southern China, and until 1957 there was no bridge across it from Yibin to Shanghai. The Central China floods of 1931 were among the deadliest natural disasters ever recorded.

The Yangtze basin is home to nearly one-third of China's population, and the river is the longest in Asia and the largest entirely within a single country. Tens of millions of people live in its floodplain, which floods naturally every summer and is habitable because dikes protect it. The Three Gorges Dam is the largest hydroelectric power station in the world by installed capacity. The basin has 416 known fish species, 178 of them found only there, and the Yangtze river dolphin, or baiji, was declared functionally extinct in 2006.
yaounde: Yaoundé lies in the Centre Region of Cameroon at an elevation of about 750 metres, between the Nyong and Sanaga rivers at the northern edge of the area's forests. It is thermally equatorial, with a narrow range of temperatures through the year, and has a long wet season from March to November with a lull in July. Two trans-African highways pass through it, and railway lines run west to the port of Douala and north to N'Gaoundéré.

The outpost of Epsumb, or Jeundo, was founded by the German explorers Lt. Richard Kund and Hans Tappenbeck, with the agreement of the chiefs of Ela Esono. From December 1889 to May 1895 the German botanist Georg August Zenker occupied it as an agricultural research station, which he named Jaunde after the local Yaunde or Ewondo people. It served as a base for the rubber and ivory trade, buying from local people in exchange for imported clothing and iron.

In 1895 Major Dominik set up a military garrison at the site, which made possible a Pallotine mission and religious school at nearby Mvolyé. During the First World War Jaunde was occupied by Belgian troops from the Congo. After Germany's defeat France held eastern Cameroon as a mandate of the League of Nations, and Yaoundé was chosen as the capital of the colony in 1922. Douala long remained the more important settlement, but Yaoundé grew rapidly after 1958, because of the cocoa crisis and unrest along the coast, and it has been the seat of government of the Republic of Cameroon since independence.

Yaoundé has more than 2.8 million inhabitants and is the second-largest city in Cameroon after Douala. Its economy is centred on the civil service and the diplomatic services, with tobacco, dairy products, beer, clay, glass goods and timber among its industries. Its landmarks include the Presidential Palace in the Etoudi district, the Palais des Congrès and the Reunification Monument. Cameroon is bilingual, with English and French both official, and the city has schools in both systems.
yashwant-rao-holkar: Yashwant Rao was the third son of Tukoji Rao Holkar. He was educated in accountancy and could read Persian, Marathi and Urdu. On 29 January 1797 Tukoji named his eldest son, Kashi Rao, as his successor. The second son, Malhar Rao, rebelled and Yashwant Rao joined him; on 14 September the army of Daulat Rao Scindia surprised their camp, Malhar Rao was killed and Yashwant Rao fled wounded. He gathered a following that included Pindharis and Afghans under Mir Khan. Claiming to act for his infant nephew Khande Rao, he declared himself head of the Holkars in January 1799, and by April had defeated Kashi Rao's commander, the Chevalier Dudrenec.

In 1799 the widows of Mahadaji Scindia asked his help to recover Ujjain and promised him four lakh rupees; he accepted five lakh from Ambaji Ingle to betray them, and looted the city. His victory over Scindia and the Peshwa on 25 October 1802, the day of Diwali, was won at Hadapsar near Pune. The Peshwa fled to Sinhagad, and Holkar took over the administration at Pune and appointed Amrutrao as Peshwa. The British, fearing for their own territories and those of their ally the Nizam of Hyderabad, decided to restore the Peshwa under their protection.

On 8 October 1804 he marched on Delhi to gain control of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and besieged it for more than a week, but could not overcome the defence under Colonel Ochterlony. The emperor nevertheless gave him the title Maharajadhiraja Raj Rajeshwar Alija Bahadur. He appealed to other Indian rulers to join him against the British, but Daulat Rao Scindia would not fight and others gave no direct help. He fled to the Sikh Empire, where Ranjit Singh refused a British request to arrest him.

By the treaty signed at Rajghat on 24 December 1805 the British returned his territory, accepted his dominion over Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bundi and undertook not to interfere in Holkar affairs; he gave up his claims to Bundelkhand and the lands north of the Chambal. He thus avoided the subsidiary alliance imposed on other Maratha chiefs. Lord Lake resigned in protest at the abandonment of the Company's Indian allies. In a letter of 15 February 1806 Holkar wrote that he had concluded the war when he found himself abandoned on all sides. He died on 28 October 1811.
yasser-arafat: Arafat was born in Cairo on 4 or 24 August 1929, the second-youngest of seven children of Palestinian parents. His father, Abdel Raouf al-Qudwa al-Husseini, was from Gaza City and worked as a textile merchant in Cairo. His mother, Zahwa Abul Saud, whose family home was Jerusalem, died in 1933. He enrolled at the University of King Fuad I in 1944 and graduated in 1950, and by 1946 was an Arab nationalist procuring weapons to be smuggled into Mandatory Palestine. When the 1948 Arab-Israeli War began he left the university and fought in the Gaza area alongside the Muslim Brotherhood, without joining it. He later served as president of the General Union of Palestinian Students from 1952 to 1956.

After the Suez Crisis of 1956 the guerrilla forces in Gaza were expelled, Arafat among them. In 1957 he obtained a visa for Kuwait, where he met Salah Khalaf and Khalil al-Wazir, who became his top aides. In the late 1950s he co-founded Fatah, a paramilitary organisation seeking Israel's replacement with a Palestinian state, which he led from 1959. He joined the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1967 and in 1969 was elected chair of the Palestinian National Council. Fatah's presence in Jordan brought clashes with King Hussein's government, and in the early 1970s it moved to Lebanon, where it took part in the Lebanese Civil War and became a target of Israeli invasions in 1978 and 1982.

From 1983 to 1993 he was based in Tunisia, and in 1985 survived an Israeli bombing of his Tunis headquarters in which 73 people died. He shifted from open conflict to negotiation, acknowledging Israel's right to exist in 1988, and took part in the Madrid Conference of 1991, the talks that led to the Oslo Accords of 1993 and the Camp David Summit of 2000. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1994 with Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres.

After being confined in his Ramallah compound by the Israeli army for over two years, Arafat fell into a coma in late 2004 and died on 11 November 2004; the cause of his death remains the subject of speculation. Palestinians generally view him as a martyr who symbolised their national aspirations, while many Israelis regarded him as a terrorist. Palestinian rivals often denounced him as corrupt or too submissive in his concessions to Israel.
yellow-river: The Yellow River, or Huang He, is the second-longest river in China and the sixth-longest in the world, an estimated 5,464 kilometres long with a drainage basin of 795,000 square kilometres. It rises in the Bayan Har Mountains and flows generally eastwards, makes the 1,500-kilometre Ordos Loop through Inner Mongolia, turns south to form the border between Shanxi and Shaanxi, turns east again at its confluence with the Wei River and crosses the North China Plain to the Bohai Sea. It is named for the yellow colour of its water, from the sediment it carries from the Loess Plateau. Chronicles indicate that the river, once simply called the river, became muddy sometime between 367 BCE and 165 CE.

The basin was the birthplace of ancient Chinese civilisation. According to traditional historiography the Xia dynasty originated on its banks around 2100 BCE, and Sima Qian's Shiji records that the Xia were founded after the tribes around the river united to fight its floods. One estimate counts 1,593 floods in the 2,540 years between 595 BCE and 1946, and the river has been nicknamed both China's Pride and China's Sorrow.

In 602 BCE it shifted several hundred kilometres east at Suxu Mouth, the first major course change recorded in history. In 1128 Song troops under the Kaifeng governor Du Chong breached the southern dikes to stop the advancing Jin army, and the river shifted south of the Shandong Peninsula into the Yellow Sea, where it flowed until 1855, merging with the Huai River. Between 1851 and 1855 it returned north, amid floods that provoked the Nien and Taiping Rebellions, and it more or less adopted its present course in the flood of 1897.

Floods of the river have killed over one million people in all. Among the deadliest were the flood of 1344 under the Yuan dynasty, the flood of 1887, which killed between 900,000 and 2 million people, and the flood of 1931, which killed an estimated 1 to 4 million and is the worst recorded flood by deaths. Flooding in 1898 left whole communities in Shandong destitute and, with the drought that followed, contributed to the rise of the Boxer movement. About 120 million people live in the basin, which holds 13 per cent of China's cultivated land.
yemen: Yemen lies in southern Arabia and covers 455,503 square kilometres, with a coastline of about 2,000 kilometres. It borders Saudi Arabia to the north and Oman to the northeast, and its territory includes the Socotra Archipelago and several Red Sea islands, among them the Hanish Islands, Kamaran and Perim. Socotra lies east of the Horn of Africa and is geographically and bio-geographically associated with Africa.

The country divides into four main regions: the coastal plains in the west, the western highlands, the eastern highlands and the Rub' al Khali in the east. The Tihamah, a very arid and flat plain along the Red Sea coast, ends abruptly at the escarpment of the western highlands. These highlands are heavily terraced and receive the highest rainfall in Arabia, from about 760 millimetres a year at Taiz to over 1,000 millimetres at Ibb.

Large settlements existed in the mountains of northern Yemen from about 5000 BCE. The four major kingdoms of South Arabia were Saba, Hadhramaut, Qataban and Ma'in. Saba, thought to be the biblical Sheba, was the most prominent, and its rulers took a title generally thought to mean unifier. It built the Great Dam of Marib around 940 BCE. A Roman army of 10,000 men under Aelius Gallus was defeated before it reached Marib.

By the third century BCE Qataban, Hadhramaut and Ma'in had become independent of Saba, which regained its hegemony after Qataban collapsed in 50 BCE. The Himyarites annexed Sanaa around 100 CE, and by 275 Shammar Yahri'sh had conquered Hadhramaut, Najran and Tihamah, unifying Yemen under Himyarite rule. By 515 Himyar was divided along religious lines, and civil turmoil brought an intervention from Aksum.

Islam spread rapidly in the seventh century, and for centuries Yemen was a primary producer of coffee, exported through the port of Mokha. In the nineteenth century the country was divided between the Ottoman and British empires. The Kingdom of Yemen was established after the First World War and became the Yemen Arab Republic in 1962. South Yemen became independent in 1967, and the two states united in 1990.

Sanaa is the constitutional capital and largest city. Modern Standard Arabic is the official language and Islam the state religion. The country has an estimated population of about 34.7 million. The old city of Sanaa, with its tower-houses of mud-brick and stone, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. Yemen is a member of the Arab League, the United Nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.
yerevan: Yerevan lies on the banks of the Hrazdan River, in the north-east of the Ararat Plain, in the central-western part of Armenia and the heart of the Armenian Highland. Its average height is 990 metres. The upper part of the city is surrounded by mountains on three sides, and the Hrazdan divides it in two through a canyon. Mount Ararat, visible from any part of the city, is its principal symbol.

The origin of the name is unknown. One theory ties it to the Armenian king Yervand (Orontes) IV, but it more likely derives from the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BCE, and the name evolved through Erevani and Erevan into Yerevan as Urartian and Armenian elements blended.

The territory has been inhabited since approximately the second half of the 4th millennium BCE. The southern district of Shengavit was populated from at least 3200 BCE in the period of the Kura–Araxes culture of the early Bronze Age, and excavations there found a series of large round buildings and ritual installations. King Argishti I of Urartu founded the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BCE at the western extreme of the Ararat Plain, as a great administrative and religious centre. By the late ancient Armenian Kingdom new capital cities were founded and Yerevan declined.

The Safavid Empire forcibly deported hundreds of thousands of Armenians to Iran in the Great Surgun of 1603–05, which mostly depopulated the city. An earthquake mostly destroyed it in 1679, and it was rebuilt on a smaller scale. It later became part of the Russian Empire. After the First World War it became the capital of the First Republic of Armenia in 1918, as thousands of survivors of the Armenian genocide in the Ottoman Empire arrived. It grew rapidly in the 20th century within the Soviet Union.

Yerevan is the capital and largest city of Armenia and one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with 1,086,677 people. It has been the capital since 1918, the fourteenth in Armenia's history. It is the seat of the Araratian Pontifical Diocese, the largest diocese of the Armenian Apostolic Church.

Erebuni Fortress is considered the birthplace of the city, and Saint Gregory Cathedral is the largest Armenian cathedral in the world. Tsitsernakaberd is the official memorial to the victims of the Armenian genocide. The Matenadaran holds one of the largest depositories of ancient books and manuscripts in the world.
yiddish: Yiddish, historically called Judeo-German or Jewish German, is a West Germanic language that originated in the Holy Roman Empire in the Middle Ages. By the 10th century a distinctive Jewish culture had formed in Central Europe, centred on the Rhineland (Mainz) and the Palatinate (notably Worms and Speyer), an area that came to be known as Ashkenaz. Yiddish gave the nascent Ashkenazi community a vernacular based on High German, fused with many elements from Hebrew, notably Mishnaic Hebrew, and to some extent Aramaic. Most varieties also include Slavic elements. It has traditionally been written in the Hebrew alphabet, and its orthography developed towards the end of the High Middle Ages.

The earliest surviving references, from the 12th century, call the language loshn-ashknaz, the language of Ashkenaz, or taytsh, a variant of the name for Middle High German. Colloquially it is mame-loshn, the mother tongue, as against loshn koydesh, the holy tongue, meaning Hebrew. The oldest surviving literary document in Yiddish is a blessing in the Worms machzor, a Hebrew prayer book, first recorded in 1272. Eastern Yiddish, far more common today, differs from Western Yiddish, which Ethnologue classifies as endangered, by its size and its extensive Slavic vocabulary.

Printing in the 16th century allowed cheap large-scale production of Yiddish works. Elia Levita, the earliest named Yiddish author, composed the Bovo-Bukh about 1507-08, printed from 1541. From the late 18th century, under the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, the language lost prestige, stigmatised by assimilationists and later by Zionists in favour of national languages and Hebrew.

In the early 20th century, especially after the October Revolution, Yiddish emerged as a major Eastern European language, with a flourishing literature, theatre and cinema, and the Yiddish Scientific Institute, YIVO, was founded in 1925. Before the Second World War there were 11 to 13 million speakers. About 85 per cent of the approximately six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust were Yiddish speakers, and the language declined massively. It is still spoken in Haredi communities, and a 2021 estimate counted 600,000 speakers in all.
york: York lies in the Vale of York, a flat area of fertile arable land bordered by the Pennines, the North York Moors and the Yorkshire Wolds. The city was built at the confluence of the Ouse and the Foss on a terminal moraine left by the last ice age. It grew up as a river port, and the Ouse was originally a tidal river accessible to the seagoing ships of the time. The Roman name Eburacum or Eboracum is a Latinisation of a Brittonic word that may mean place of yew trees, or alternatively property of a man named Eburos.

Archaeological evidence suggests that Mesolithic people settled in the area between 8000 and 7000 BCE. By the time of the Roman conquest the land was held by a tribe the Romans called the Brigantes, whose territory first became a client state. Its leaders later grew hostile, and the Ninth Legion was sent north of the Humber into it. The city was founded as Eboracum in 71 CE. It became the capital of Britannia Inferior, a province of the Roman Empire, and was later the capital of the kingdoms of Deira and Northumbria and of Scandinavian York.

In 1068, two years after the Norman invasion, the people of York rebelled. The rising succeeded at first, but William the Conqueror suppressed it on arriving and at once built a wooden fortress on a motte. After a second rebellion in 1069 he built another timber castle across the Ouse. Both were destroyed in 1069 and rebuilt about the time of his ravaging of Northumbria, the Harrying of the North, when he destroyed everything from York to Durham.

York declined economically in the Tudor period. The Dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII ended its monastic houses. This contributed to the Pilgrimage of Grace, an uprising of northern Catholics, and Henry restored his authority by setting up the Council of the North in the dissolved St Mary's Abbey. The railway promoter George Hudson brought the railway to York in 1839, and the city was a major railway centre by the late 19th century.

York is a cathedral city in North Yorkshire, the traditional county town of Yorkshire. Its minster, castle and city walls are all Grade I listed. The walls are the most complete in England and incorporate part of the Roman fortress wall. York Minster is a large Gothic cathedral, and the Jorvik Viking Centre and the National Railway Museum are among the city's museums.
yugoslavia: The idea of a common state for all South Slavic peoples emerged in the late 17th century and gained prominence through the Illyrian Movement of the 19th century. The name combines the Slavic words jug, south, and Slaveni, Slavs. After the 1917 Corfu Declaration between the Yugoslav Committee and the government of the Kingdom of Serbia, the Kingdom of Serbia merged in 1918 with the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, after centuries of foreign rule under the Ottoman Empire and the Habsburg monarchy. The kingdom gained international recognition on 13 July 1922 and was renamed the Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929.

On 6 January 1929 King Alexander I abolished the constitution, banned national political parties and assumed executive power; he was assassinated in 1934, and Prince Paul acted as regent. Paul signed the Tripartite Pact on 25 March 1941, and army officers overthrew him two days later, giving the 17-year-old King Peter full powers. German, Italian and Hungarian forces invaded on 6 April 1941, and the Axis powers split the country up. The Independent State of Croatia, ruled by the fascist Ustaše, persecuted and murdered around 300,000 Serbs, along with at least 30,000 Jews and Roma.

The Communist-led Partisans proclaimed a Democratic Federal Yugoslavia, and on 29 November 1945 the Constituent Assembly proclaimed a federal republic, abolishing the monarchy. Josip Broz Tito ruled from 1944 until his death on 4 May 1980. He broke with Stalin in 1948 and in 1961 helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. The country took the name Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 7 April 1963, with six republics and the provinces of Kosovo and Vojvodina within Serbia.

After Tito's death ethnic tensions grew. Croatia and Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, Macedonia in September 1991, and Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence was recognised in April 1992. Wars followed, notably in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the war lasted more than three years and ended with the Dayton Agreement of 14 December 1995. Serbia and Montenegro formed a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on 27 April 1992, renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003, and Montenegro became independent in June 2006. Serbo-Croatian has since diverged into four standard varieties, Bosnian, Croatian, Montenegrin and Serbian, and some people from the former Yugoslavia still describe themselves as Yugoslavs.
yunnan: Yunnan is the most south-western province of China, with the Tropic of Cancer running through its southern part. It covers about 394,000 km2, 4.1 percent of the country's area. The north belongs to the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau, with a canyon region in the west and a plateau region in the east. It shares a border of 4,060 km with Myanmar, Laos and Vietnam, holds nine lakes of more than 30 km2, among them Dianchi near Kunming and Erhai near Dali, and is China's most biologically diverse province.

The Yuanmou Man, a Homo erectus fossil, is dated to about 1.7 million years ago. Around the 3rd century BCE the area near present-day Kunming was known as Dian, and the Chu general Zhuang Qiao set himself up as King of Dian. The Han dynasty conquered Dian in 109 BCE and founded the Yizhou commandery. In the 320s CE the Cuan clan migrated in, and ruled eastern Yunnan for over four hundred years. Around Lake Erhai six local regimes called zhao emerged; the southernmost, Mengshe, became Nanzhao, which lasted from 738 to 937.

In 937 Duan Siping founded the Dali Kingdom, which the Mongol Empire conquered in 1253 after King Duan Xingzhi defected. In 1273 Kublai Khan appointed Ajall Shams al-Din Omar as governor. The Ming dynasty destroyed the Yuan loyalists and the remnants of the House of Duan by the early 1380s and installed Mu Ying and his family as hereditary aristocrats. Under the Ming and Qing large areas were run under the native chieftain system. After 1911 local warlords governed with unusual autonomy, financing themselves through opium.

Yunnan has about 47 million people, and its capital is Kunming. From the Yuan dynasty two major waves of migration from Han-majority areas reached the province. Ethnic minorities make up about 34 percent of the population; the main groups are the Yi, Bai, Hani, Zhuang, Dai and Miao. Yunnan has been identified as the birthplace of tea.
yuri-gagarin: Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin was born on 9 March 1934 in the village of Klushino, in the Russian SFSR, the third of four children of a carpenter and a dairy farmer who worked on a sovkhoz. The Germans captured Klushino on 18 October 1941, burned down the school and 27 houses and forced the residents to work the farms. The Gagarins spent 21 months in a mud hut behind their house until the occupation ended, and in early 1943 his two elder siblings were deported to Poland for slave labour.

In 1950, aged 16, he began an apprenticeship as a foundryman at a steel plant in Lyubertsy, near Moscow. He then studied tractors at the Industrial Technical School in Saratov, where he volunteered at a local flying club. In 1955 he was accepted to the First Chkalov Higher Air Force Pilots School in Orenburg, and on 5 November 1957 he was commissioned a lieutenant in the Soviet Air Forces.

After the launch of Luna 3 in October 1959 he expressed interest in space exploration. Sergei Korolev, the chief engineer of the Vostok programme, specified that candidates should weigh under 72 kg and be no taller than 1.70 metres to fit the capsule; Gagarin was 1.57 metres tall. He was among the first twelve cosmonauts approved on 7 March 1960.

On 12 April 1961, travelling on Vostok 1 and launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome, he completed one orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes and became the first person in space. Nikita Khrushchev awarded him the title Hero of the Soviet Union. He toured widely abroad, accepting invitations from about 30 countries. Vostok 1 was his only spaceflight: he was backup crew to Soyuz 1, in which his friend Vladimir Komarov was killed, and Soviet officials then banned him from further flights.

On 27 March 1968, on a routine training flight, Gagarin and the flight instructor Vladimir Seryogin died when their MiG-15UTI crashed near the town of Kirzhach. Their ashes were interred in the Kremlin wall. The cause of the crash is uncertain. At least three investigations were held, and a KGB report declassified in March 2003 blamed out-of-date weather information and external fuel tanks left on the aircraft.

The date of his flight, 12 April, has been marked as Cosmonautics Day since 1962 in the Soviet Union and since 1991 in Russia and some other former Soviet republics. In 2011 the United Nations declared it the International Day of Human Space Flight.
yury-of-moscow: Yury Danilovich was the eldest son of Daniel of Moscow, the first prince of Moscow. His first military action was the defence of Pereslavl-Zalessky against Andrey of Gorodets, grand prince of Vladimir. Because Daniel had never held the grand princely title, his descendants had no legitimate claim to Vladimir under the traditional rules of succession. When Andrey died on 27 July 1304, Tokhta, khan of the Golden Horde, therefore gave the title to Yury's uncle, Mikhail of Tver. Yury rebelled, and two campaigns by Mikhail against Moscow, in 1305 and 1308, forced him to accept the khan's decision.

Yury meanwhile arranged the murder of Prince Konstantin of Ryazan, whom his father had captured in 1302 and held in Moscow, and annexed the Ryazan fortress of Kolomna. He also took Mozhaisk, which had belonged to the princes of Smolensk. By 1314 he had the backing of Metropolitan Peter and a military alliance with Novgorod against Tver.

In 1315 he went to the Horde, where he spent two years. His bride Konchaka converted to Orthodox Christianity and was baptised Agafiia. Returning with a large force of Tatars, he approached Tver, but his army was defeated and his wife and his brother Boris were captured; he fled to Novgorod and sued for peace. When his wife died unexpectedly as a hostage in Tver, he told the khan that Mikhail had ordered her poisoned. Both princes were summoned to Sarai, and after a trial Mikhail was executed on 22 November 1318.

As grand prince from 1318 to 1322 Yury was resisted by other princes and by the people, who thought his appointment illegitimate. He was charged with gathering the tribute for the Horde, and in his last two years in the office the khan sent no fewer than four punitive expeditions to the northeastern principalities to enforce it.

In 1322 Dmitry of Tver persuaded the khan at Sarai that Yury had kept a large part of the tribute, and received the patent for Vladimir himself. Yury then led the army of Novgorod against the Swedes, founded a fort at the mouth of the Neva River, signed the Treaty of Orekhovo in 1323 and conquered Velikiy Ustyug the same year. Summoned to the Horde for trial, he was killed by Dmitry on 21 November 1325 before any formal investigation. Dmitry was executed at the Horde eight months later. Early in 1326 Yury's remains were brought to Moscow and buried by the bishops under Metropolitan Peter.
yusuf-adil-shah: Yusuf was born in 1450, and accounts of his origin differ. He may have been a Georgian slave purchased by Mahmud Gawan, the Bahmani prime minister; other historians call him Persian or Turkmen, and one theory makes him a Turkman of the Aq-Quyunlu. The historian Firishta presents him as a son of the Ottoman sultan Murad II, a story that modern historians consider unfounded. The Portuguese knew him as Hidalcão.

He rose quickly in the Bahmani sultan's favour and was made governor of Daulatabad; Mahmood Shah Bahmani II gave him the title Adil Khan. He led the foreigners, the Afaqis, in their conflict with the local nobility, the Deccanis, a struggle in which Mahmud Gawan was put to death in 1481. Yusuf then left Daulatabad to seize Gawan's former territories of Bijapur and Belgaum, and soon came into conflict with Malik Naib, leader of the Deccani party.

He and his son Ismail did not place the title Shah before their names but kept Adil Khan, out of respect for the Bahmanis; Ibrahim Adil Shah I formally claimed independence in 1538 and was the first of the line to use it. At Bijapur Yusuf built the citadel, the Arkilla, and the palace called the Faroukh Mahal. He invited poets and artisans from Persia, Turkey and Rome to his court and was himself an accomplished musician and scholar.

He was killed in the Battle of Koilkonda against Vijayanagara on 5 December 1510, a few days after the loss of Goa. His son Ismail Adil Shah, a minor, succeeded him, aided in his rule by a certain Kamal Khan. Yusuf had married Punji, sister of the Maratha lord Mukundrao Kadam, who was renamed Bubuji Khanum; their daughters married the sultans of Ahmednagar and Berar and a Bahmani prince. The sultanate he founded lasted for close to two centuries, until Aurangzeb ended it in 1686.
